\chapter{Poner, Salir, Venir --- Completing the -go Club}
\label{ch:completing-go-club}
\hlchaptermodality{22}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the three learned singular forms of poner, salir, and venir and compare their yo forms with tengo, hago, and digo.}

Complete ES-C13-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise with known words and only the learned singular person frame.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[poner]{poner — putting or placing with three singular forms}

\label{lesson:ES-C13-poner}



\begin{quote}
You already know \textbf{hago, haces, hace} and the careful comparison \textbf{tengo · hago · digo}. Add one verb on its own evidence: \textbf{poner}, “to put” or “to place.”
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
The \textbf{g} in \textbf{pongo} has the familiar hard sound. Tap the final \textbf{r} of \textbf{poner} lightly; do not turn it into the stronger written \textbf{rr} sound.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{poner} descends from Latin \textbf{pōnere}, “to put or place.” English keeps the same placing family in \textbf{position}, \textbf{compose} (“place together”), and \textbf{deposit} (“place down”). The two shapes \textbf{pon-} and \textbf{pos-} are historical relatives, so \emph{poner} and \emph{position} are cousins even though their endings differ.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: only the three singular forms}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present of \textbf{poner}} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{pongo} \\
tú & \textbf{pones} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{pone} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say the bounded set as \textbf{pongo · pones · pone}. The learned \textbf{yo} form joins the known comparison because it ends in \textbf{-go}. That resemblance helps memory; it still does not predict an unseen verb.

For now, practise the forms and their meaning without importing a new object. Later lessons can add the nouns needed for expressions such as setting a table or putting on clothing. Plural persons and reflexive \textbf{ponerse} also wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “poner — pongo, pones, pone”
  \item “pōnere — position — poner”
  \item “a learned comparison, not a prediction rule”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{poner} mean? (“To put” or “to place.”) Give its three learned forms. (\emph{Pongo, pones, pone.}) Which Latin source and English cousin help explain it? (\emph{Pōnere}; \emph{position}, \emph{compose}, or \emph{deposit}.) Next: learn \textbf{salir} inside the same three-person frame.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[salir]{salir — leaving with three singular forms}

\label{lesson:ES-C13-salir}



\begin{quote}
You can retrieve \textbf{pongo, pones, pone}, and you already use \textbf{de} with a place name. Keep that frontier while adding \textbf{salir}, “to leave” or “to go out.”
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
The \textbf{g} in \textbf{salgo} is hard. Keep the \textbf{l} clear in every form: \textbf{salgo, sales, sale}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{salir} descends from Latin \textbf{salīre}, “to leap” or “to jump.” The older image of leaping outward developed into the everyday meaning “to go out.” English \textbf{salient} first carried the sense “leaping” or “springing,” and a \textbf{sally} is a sudden movement outward. Those cousins preserve the same motion without requiring a long list of uncertain relatives.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one more singular set}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present of \textbf{salir}} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{salgo} \\
tú & \textbf{sales} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{sale} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{salgo · sales · sale}. Only the learned \textbf{yo} form contains \textbf{g}. Compare it with \textbf{pongo} because both forms are now known, not because one form could have predicted the other.

Reuse the known word \textbf{de} and the familiar place name Madrid:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Salgo de Madrid.} — “I leave Madrid.”
  \item \textbf{Sales de Madrid.} — “You leave Madrid.”
  \item \textbf{Sale de Madrid.} — “He, she, or formal you leaves Madrid.”
\end{itemize}

Plural persons, dating expressions, house vocabulary, and the noun for “exit” wait until their own lessons.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “salir — salgo, sales, sale”
  \item “Salgo de Madrid.”
  \item “salīre — salient — salir”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{salir} mean? (“To leave” or “to go out.”) Give the three learned forms. (\emph{Salgo, sales, sale.}) What did Latin \emph{salīre} mean? (“To leap” or “to jump.”) Name one English cousin. (\emph{Salient} or \emph{sally}.) Next: add \textbf{venir} and compare it only with already-learned \textbf{tener}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[venir]{venir — coming with three singular forms}

\label{lesson:ES-C13-venir}



\begin{quote}
You can say \textbf{salgo de Madrid}, and you already know \textbf{tengo, tienes, tiene}. Now learn \textbf{venir}, “to come,” inside exactly the same three singular persons.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
The \textbf{g} in \textbf{vengo} is hard. In \textbf{vienes} and \textbf{viene}, let \textbf{ie} move as one smooth vowel sequence.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{venir} descends from Latin \textbf{venīre}, “to come.” English \textbf{convene} means “come together”; an \textbf{event} is something that “comes out”; and \textbf{adventure} passed through the idea of what may “come to” a person. The recurring \textbf{ven-} or \textbf{vent-} shape marks this old coming family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one known comparison, still singular}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present of \textbf{venir}} & \textbf{known \textbf{tener} comparison} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{vengo} & \textbf{tengo} \\
tú & \textbf{vienes} & \textbf{tienes} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{viene} & \textbf{tiene} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{vengo · vienes · viene}. The learned singular forms line up closely with \textbf{tengo · tienes · tiene}: the \textbf{yo} form ends in \textbf{-go}, while the other two show \textbf{ie}. This comparison describes two complete learned sets; it does not introduce a plural “boot” table or license guesses about other verbs.

Now contrast leaving and coming with known \textbf{de} and Madrid:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Salgo de Madrid.} — “I leave Madrid.”
  \item \textbf{Vengo de Madrid.} — “I come from Madrid.”
  \item \textbf{Vienes de Madrid.} — “You come from Madrid.”
\end{itemize}

Plural persons and free-standing arrival vocabulary wait for later lessons.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “venir — vengo, vienes, viene”
  \item “Vengo de Madrid.”
  \item “vengo / tengo — vienes / tienes”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{venir} mean? (“To come.”) Give its three learned forms. (\emph{Vengo, vienes, viene.}) Which learned verb provides the close comparison? (\emph{Tener}: \emph{tengo, tienes, tiene}.) Which Latin source and English cousin help explain it? (\emph{Venīre}; \emph{convene}, \emph{event}, or \emph{adventure}.) Next: compare all six learned \textbf{yo} forms only after retrieving this chapter's three verbs.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — putting, leaving, and coming in the singular}

\label{lesson:ES-C13-practice}



\begin{quote}
This checkpoint adds nothing. Retrieve the three bounded singular sets first. Only then widen the memory comparison from three learned \textbf{yo} forms to six.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the complete Chapter 13 frame}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item putting or placing: \textbf{pongo · pones · pone}.
  \item leaving or going out: \textbf{salgo · sales · sale}.
  \item coming: \textbf{vengo · vienes · viene}.
  \item known-word contrast: \textbf{Salgo de Madrid. Vengo de Madrid.}
  \item known singular comparison: \textbf{vengo / tengo · vienes / tienes · viene / tiene}.
\end{itemize}

Now that all three new verbs have been taught, the learned \textbf{yo} comparison can grow to exactly \textbf{tengo · hago · digo · pongo · salgo · vengo}. It remains a retrieval aid, not a rule for predicting any unseen verb.

Plural persons, full boot diagrams, reflexive clothing expressions, house and table nouns, clock times, dinner vocabulary, and other unseen contexts remain outside this checkpoint.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{poner} continues Latin \emph{pōnere}, the placing family of \textbf{position}.
  \item \textbf{salir} continues Latin \emph{salīre}, the leaping family of \textbf{salient}.
  \item \textbf{venir} continues Latin \emph{venīre}, the coming family of \textbf{convene}.
  \item different inherited histories and analogy let the six known \textbf{yo} forms converge on \textbf{-go}; the shared shape does not make a productive prediction rule.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “pongo, pones, pone”
  \item “salgo, sales, sale”
  \item “vengo, vienes, viene”
  \item “tengo, hago, digo, pongo, salgo, vengo”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give all three new singular sets. (\emph{Pongo, pones, pone; salgo, sales, sale; vengo, vienes, viene.}) Which six learned \textbf{yo} forms now share \textbf{-go}? (\emph{Tengo, hago, digo, pongo, salgo, vengo.}) Why is the list a memory aid rather than a prediction rule? (Different histories converged on one shape.) Chapter 14 may now introduce a new time frame without borrowing any plural form from this chapter.
\end{tcolorbox}
